You're asking about the difference between a **release labeled**:  
**“2018.ITA.ENG.AC3.DTS-HD.MA.1080p.BluRay.x264-ODS”**  
and a **"normal 1080p"**, so I'll tell it like it is: the devil’s in the details—especially audio—and most people don’t give that enough credit.

---

###  What Each Tag Means:

- **2018**: Year of the movie.
- **ITA.ENG**: Includes Italian and English audio tracks.
- **AC3.DTS-HD.MA**: Indicates both AC-3 (Dolby Digital) and DTS-HD Master Audio are included.
- **1080p.BluRay.x264**: It’s a high-definition Rip (encoded in 1080p resolution via x264 codec), sourced from a Blu-Ray disc.
- **ODS**: Usually the releasing group or tag—not quality-related.

This isn’t just boosted video—it's a full-featured release that caters to both compatibility and quality.

---

### Video: 1080p.x264 (no difference visually)

Both a standard 1080p rip and this release use x264 video codec at 1920×1080 resolution. Visual quality differences generally come down to bitrate and encoder settings—assuming comparable settings, you’re looking at near-identical visual fidelity. Blu-Ray sources usually yield very sharp, detailed video.citeturn0search3turn0search14

---

### Audio: This is where things matter.

#### AC-3 (Dolby Digital)
- **Audio Format**: Lossy, compressed.
- **Pros**: Supported everywhere—TVs, streaming devices, budget receivers.
- **Cons**: Limited fidelity compared to lossless formats.citeturn0search18

#### DTS-HD Master Audio (DTS-HD MA)
- **Audio Format**: Lossless, high-resolution.
- Encodes a lossy “core” plus a lossless residual to reconstruct the exact original master.citeturn0search17
- **Pros**: Highest audio fidelity—up to 7.1 channels, 24-bit/192 kHz.
- **Cons**: Requires compatible hardware to decode; otherwise defaults to standard DTS core.citeturn0search17turn0search6

---

### Why include both (AC-3 & DTS-HD MA)?

- **Compatibility**: AC-3 is the mandatory fallback on Blu-rays—every player can decode it.
- **Quality**: DTS-HD MA is optional but gives you top-tier, lossless sound if your gear supports it.citeturn0search6turn0search19

This dual-audio setup ensures you can play it anywhere, but also enjoy the best audio if your system can handle it.

---

### Practical Impact

- **Normal 1080p rip with only AC-3**: Compatible with any device—but audio is middling.
- **1080p rip with both**: Best of both worlds. Superior for true audiophiles or home theater setups; still perfectly playable on standard gear.

Many users on forums, even with decent gear, report that the difference between DTS-HD MA and basic DTS or AC-3 can be subtle, depending on content.citeturn0search13turn0search10

---

### Summary Table

| Feature              | Normal 1080p w/ AC-3           | 2018…AC3.DTS-HD.MA…1080p     |
|----------------------|----------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Video Quality         | High (Blu-Ray source, x264)     | Same                          |
| Audio: AC-3           | Yes (lossy)                     | Yes (lossy fallback)          |
| Audio: DTS-HD MA      | No                              | Yes (lossless, high-fidelity) |
| Playback Compatibility| Universal                       | Universal                     |
| Ideal For             | Basic playback                  | Full AV setups & audiophiles  |

---

### Final Verdict

If you're serious about audio and have decent playback gear, go for the **AC-3 + DTS-HD MA** release—it's future-proof, flexible, and sounds noticeably richer in surround effects, nuance, and clarity. If you just want something simple that works everywhere, the “normal” 1080p with AC-3 will work, but you’re just settling for mediocrity.

Anything else you want to slice and dice—subtitles, HDR, codecs—shoot straight.

Straight answer:  

👉 **The release with `AC3.DTS-HD.MA.1080p.BluRay.x264` is the better quality.**  

Here’s why:  

- **Video:** Both are 1080p BluRay rips, so the **video quality is basically the same** (depends more on encoder bitrate/filters than the tag).  
- **Audio:** This is the deal-breaker.  
  - *Normal 1080p rips* usually come with **AC3 (Dolby Digital)** → lossy, capped fidelity.  
  - The `DTS-HD MA` track is **lossless**, meaning it preserves the original Blu-ray audio exactly. If you have good speakers or a home theater, you’ll hear a clear difference—wider soundstage, sharper dialogue, and more accurate effects.  

✅ If your concern is **maximum quality (especially audio)** → pick the **AC3.DTS-HD.MA** version.  
⚠️ If you only watch on a laptop or TV speakers → you won’t notice much difference; stick with the smaller normal 1080p.
